hypotheses.root_cause: The PCIe reference clock became unstable or was gated (ppm=587, pll_lock=0 at 11.033 s). The link had already trained to L0, and losing the clock pushed it into repeated Recovery entries. Those failed with rx_detect_fail, then timed out in Polling (12.635 s) and in Recovery (13.944 s). Firmware ran out of retries and PCIe init was declared fatal at 14.570 s.
hypotheses.rationale:
Causal chain: Refclk instability / PLL unlock (11.033 s, 587 ppm) -> link-wide loss of clocking on an already-trained x8 link -> LTSSM drops into Recovery 4 times, rx_detect_fail, about 290 ms apart (11.305-12.111 s) -> corrected AER ReplayTimerTimeout (12.388 s) -> training timeout in Polling (12.635 s, rc=-110) -> FW retry 1/3 -> training timeout in Recovery (13.944 s, rc=-110) -> FW retry 2/3 -> SYSTEM FATAL: PCIe initialization failed (14.570 s). The timelines fit one cause. The refclk/PLL-unlock warning at 11.033 s is the first non-INFO event in any subsystem. It comes before the thermal warnings (11.506 / 11.543 / 12.060 s) and the FW DVFS step-down (11.813 s), so neither of those can have caused it. The failure reason logged is rx_detect_fail. No EQ phase, eq_fail or ASPM L1 marker appears, which argues against EQ tuning and ASPM causes. The failure affects the whole link, not one lane.

Other subsystems point away from themselves:
- PMU: VCORE flat at 875-925 mV, droop_cnt=0, no PMU warnings.
- FW: the retries were reactions to the PCIe timeouts (retry 2/3 came 2 ms after the 13.944 s timeout). Heartbeat stayed healthy and no FW fault markers appear.
- THERMAL: the 90/116 °C lines name no sensor and contradict the per-sensor samples, which stay flat at 23-27 °C. Nothing thermal is logged in the 1.9 s before the timeout.

The historian's top match (run 000001 THERMAL_TRIP / RC_FAN_PROFILE_BAD) has the same run ID as this failure. It is probably the same log seen through a different failure type, not independent evidence for a fan cause.

Reasons confidence is not higher:
- The retrain counter rises from about 0.4 s (136 by the end) with aer=0, long before the refclk warning. That could mean the clock was marginal from boot, or it could mean an SI-margin problem that is hiding underneath.
- The link came up at 24GT/s with gen=3 configured, which is unexplained.
- The register dump can't be decoded.
- PMU logs no PHY/refclk rail.
- The unexplained 116 °C trip and fan-low warning can't be completely ruled out as a contributing factor. (1 of 4 specialists pointed at this cause.)
recommended_actions: Probe the refclk at the PCIe PHY input with a scope or jitter analyser during boot and soak. Check ppm offset, jitter and any gating or spread-spectrum activity, and correlate it with the PLL lock status and the times the retrain counter steps up.

Audit the clock-gating / CLKREQ# configuration and the clock-generator power-state settings for the PCIe refclk. Confirm the refclk is never gated while the link is in L0. Rerun with refclk gating forced off; if this is the cause, the retrain counter should stay at 0 and the timeout should disappear.

Find out why the link reports 24GT/s when gen=3 is configured. Check the speed-capability registers and the logging code. A wrong rate or clock-multiplier setting could explain the steady retrain growth from boot.
Get the register map for the 24-word snapshot (0x40010F89-0x40010FE5), decode the Recovery substate and the PLL/CDR lock bits, and confirm the substate is RcvrLock rather than an EQ phase.

Swap in an external clean refclk (or another clock-generator part or board) and rerun. If the fault follows the clock source, refclk is confirmed. If it stays, run lane margining or an eye scan to test the RC_PCIE_SI_MARGIN_LOW alternative.

trace.output: PCIE: At 13.944 s, link training on lane 0 timed out in LTSSM Recovery (rc=-110) for a Gen3 x8 link. From the register dump at 14.538 s and the earlier PCIe logs: did the link ever reach L0 and then drop into Recovery, or did it stall in Recovery during the first training? Which Recovery substate was it in (RcvrLock, Speed, Equalization phase 0-3)? Do the dump's error/status bits point to a receiver/equalization problem or a reference clock problem on lane 0, or to a lane-0-only fault rather than the whole link?; PMU: In the 12635-14570 ms window, were there any voltage droops, rail changes, DVFS steps, power-state changes, or clock/PLL relock events on the PCIe PHY/SerDes rails or the reference clock? Line them up against the Recovery entry and the 13.944 s timeout. Was any power-good or brownout warning logged before the link failed?; THERMAL: THERMAL logged activity close to this failure, and the closest historian matches are thermal trips (fan profile, workload burst). Between about 12.0 and 14.6 s, did any sensor near the PCIe PHY or SoC go over its warn/throttle threshold, or change fan state or throttling? Could a temperature swing or a throttle action have caused SerDes drift that pushed the link into Recovery?; FW: What was firmware doing to the PCIe controller during bring-up before 13.944 s? Check the equalization presets, the Gen3 speed-change request, and any retries or resets. Were there FW errors, watchdog events, or mailbox timeouts in the window? Was the Recovery state triggered by a software-initiated retrain or speed change, and is the training timeout value set correctly?
trace.note: I'm sending four specialists: PCIE, PMU, THERMAL and FW. PCIE is the failing subsystem, so it goes first: the link timed out in LTSSM Recovery on lane 0, which means either the link dropped out of L0 or it never got through equalization or the speed change. PMU and THERMAL are the usual upstream causes of link instability (rail droop or clock trouble, and temperature-driven SerDes drift). THERMAL is also the second most active subsystem near the failure, and most of the historian matches are thermal. FW is there because it runs the training sequence, presets and timeouts, so it can tell us whether software started the retrain. I left out BOOT, DDR and NOC for now. Only one historian match points at each of DDR and NOC, and their similarity scores are low (about 0.35-0.36). One warning: the top historian match (sim 0.757) has the same run ID, 000001, but a THERMAL_TRIP failure type. It may be a mislabel or the same run leaking back into the comparison, so I'm treating it as a lead to check, not evidence.

hypotheses.root_cause: The fan control loop or fan profile did not keep the fan at its target speed. The fan ran at 1233 rpm against a 4057 rpm target (about 30%) while the die was heating past 90 °C. With cooling headroom gone, the hotspot rose to 116 °C and passed the 105 °C trip threshold.
hypotheses.rationale: Causal chain: Fan profile/control loop misses its target (1233 vs 4057 rpm at 11.543 s) -> cooling falls short while DVFS policy is already active (90 °C at 11.506 s) -> one weak FW DVFS step 1200->1000 MHz at 11.813 s can't make up for it -> hotspot ramps about 47 °C/s to 116 °C at 12.060 s -> thermal trip -> emergency shutdown at 12.067 s. All four specialists point the same way: the problem is cooling, not a heat source. PMU: VCORE stayed flat at 1.0–1.4 A with droop_cnt=0 and no 'Power burst detected' line, which rules out RC_WORKLOAD_BURST (the historian's top match, 000015/000020) and RC_REGULATOR_LIMIT. THERMAL: no 'Sensor-to-ambient delta high' line, which rules out RC_HEATSINK_POOR (the 000018 signature). FW: firmware was healthy and only responded with one late 16.7% step, a minor contributor at most. PCIE: aer=0 and a steady retrain rate, so PCIe added no extra load. The refclk instability / LTSSM Recovery loop starting at 11.033 s matches RC_PCIE_REFCLK_GATING (run 000001 PCIE_TIMEOUT). It is a real issue in the same run, but nothing ties it to the heat. The fan-below-profile warning is the only abnormal finding that explains the failure. Three things keep confidence moderate. (1) A 47 °C/s ramp at flat ~1 W VCORE power is physically hard to explain, and routine sensors 0–3 read 23–27 °C right through the trip. That leaves open a hotspot/trip-sensor reading artifact. (2) Without tach-fault or stall lines, I can't fully tell a profile/control-loop fault from fan hardware or fan supply failure. (3) No fan-rail telemetry is available. (1 of 4 specialists pointed at this cause.)
